en: The Section on the Pravāraṇā (Pravāraṇāvastu) Pravā-v 1.1.1–3: [The introductory section concerning the invitation ceremony.]
The Sanskrit text for Pravā-v 1.2.1–3 is lost.
Pravā-v 1.3: Sanskrit text lost Pravā-v 2.1–2: Sanskrit text lost
The Sanskrit text for Pravā-v 2.3.1 is lost.
The Sanskrit text is lost.

After that, a monk who is to perform the *pravāraṇā* should be appointed. A monk endowed with five qualities who has not been appointed as the *pravāraṇā*-performer should not be appointed; and one who has been appointed should be removed. What are these five?
He goes out of desire, he goes out of hatred, he goes out of delusion, he goes out of fear, and he does not know the invitation ceremony (*pravāraṇā*) nor the non-invitation ceremony.
A monk who acts as an inviter (*pravāraka*) and who is endowed with these five qualities—if unappointed, he should not be appointed; if already appointed, he should be dismissed.

A monk endowed with five qualities who has not been appointed as the *pravāraka* (the one who conducts the invitation ceremony) should be appointed; once appointed, he should not be dismissed. What are these five? He does not act out of desire, nor out of hatred, nor out of delusion, nor out of fear; and he knows both the invitation ceremony (*pravāraṇā*) and the non-invitation ceremony (*apravāraṇā*). Endowed with these five qualities...
A monk who is the *pravāraka* (the one who performs the invitation ceremony) and has not been appointed should be appointed; and once appointed, he must not be dismissed.
Furthermore, he should be appointed in this manner: having prepared the bedding and seating, as previously described, up until he has been encouraged [to undertake the task].

"Are you, [name], able to perform the *pravāraṇā* for the Saṃgha? If he is able, he should say, "I am able. (Pravā-v 2.3.2.3.1) Thereafter, one monk, having made a formal motion (*jñapti*), should carry out the ritual act (*karman*): "May the venerable Saṃgha listen."
This monk named so-and-so is willing to conduct the invitation ceremony for the Saṃgha.
If it seems the right time to the Saṃgha, may the Saṃgha grant its permission that the Saṃgha appoint this monk named so-and-so as the *pravāraka*.
This monk named so-and-so shall conduct the invitation ceremony for the Saṃgha. This is the formal motion (*jñapti*).

And the ritual action (*karman*) should be performed in this manner: "May the venerable Saṃgha listen. A monk named so-and-so, acting as the *pravāraka*, is capable of conducting the invitation (*pravāraṇā*) for the Saṃgha. Therefore, let the Saṃgha [authorize] the monk named so-and-so as the *pravāraka*..."
The Saṃgha should appoint a monk as the *pravāraka*. "This monk, named so-and-so, shall conduct the *pravāraṇā* for the Saṃgha.

Those venerable ones who consent to appoint this monk, named so-and-so, as the *pravāraka*—that this monk, named so-and-so, shall conduct the *pravāraṇā* for the Saṃgha—let them remain silent. Those who do not consent should speak."

The Saṃgha has consented that the monk named so-and-so shall be the *pravāraka*. This monk named so-and-so, as the *pravāraka*, will perform the *pravāraṇā* for the Saṃgha. It is approved and authorized by the Saṃgha;
since there is silence, I hold it to be so.
Pravā-v 2.3.3.1.
Sanskrit text lost. Pravā-v 2.3.3.2.
Sanskrit text lost, Pravā-v 2.3.3.3: ...
Pay attention, Venerable One: today is the fifteenth-day invitation (*pravāraṇā*) of the Saṃgha; it is also for me, the monk named so-and-so.
The invitation ceremony (*pravāraṇā*) is held on the fifteenth day. I, the monk named so-and-so, invite [the Saṃgha] through these three points:

what has been seen, what has been heard, and what is suspected. May the venerable ones exhort me; may the venerable ones instruct me. Out of compassion, being compassionate, may they act out of compassion. Knowing and seeing my offense, may they deal with it according to the Dharma and according to the Vinaya.
"I shall remedy it. Thus a second time, and thus a third time. ... (extant text from SHT 4473r1).
Pravā-v J 2.3.3.4.
/// One who is to be invited by means of an invitation should be invited. /// (SHT 4473r2).
(Pravā-v 150) [The monks] should perform the *pravāraṇā*; after that, the nuns perform the *pravāraṇā*.
Pravāraṇā-vastu J 2.3.3.6. ... everyone should say: "It is well that the invitation has been performed. (SHT 4473r4). Pravāraṇā-vastu J 2.3.4.

[Having sat down... "Is it possible, venerable sir, [to do so] in this way? The Venerable Upāli asked the Buddha, the Blessed One: "Venerable sir, how many formal acts of *pravāraṇā* are there? There are four."
Upāli, they act unlawfully while being divided; they act unlawfully while being united; they act lawfully while being divided; they act lawfully while being united. (Extant text from SHT 4473v1).
*Pravāraṇāvastu* J 3.2.
In that regard, there is one legal *pravāraṇā* ceremony, namely when they perform the *pravāraṇā* legally while being in concord. (Extant text from SHT 4473v2).
*Pravā-v* J 4.1.
Then, on that very fifteenth day of the *pravāraṇā*, the Blessed One sat before the community of monks on the prepared seat.

Having sat down upon that seat, the Blessed One addressed the monks: "The night is passing away, monks; perform the *pravāraṇā*, monks. Then a certain monk, rising from his seat, draped his upper robe over one shoulder, and bowing with palms joined toward the Blessed One, said this to the Blessed One: "In a certain residence, Venerable Sir..."

"A monk is afflicted, suffering, and gravely ill. How should we attend to him? The Blessed One said, "The invitation (*pravāraṇā*) should be brought for him. When the Blessed One had said, "The invitation should be brought," the monks did not know how it should be brought. The Blessed One said, "One person may bring it for one; one person may bring it for two; [one person may bring it] for many, as many as there are."
or is able to proclaim their names in the midst of the Saṃgha.
(Pravā-v 151) Pravā-v J 4.2.
"Monks, I shall prescribe the rules of proper conduct for a monk who receives the *pravāraṇā*.

The monk receiving the *pravāraṇā* should arrange his upper robe over one shoulder, remove his sandals, perform the formal salutation according to seniority, squat down, and, having joined his palms in reverence, speak as follows: 'Venerable sir, please attend to me; today is the *pravāraṇā* of the Saṃgha.'"

It is the fifteenth day. For me, a monk of such-and-such a name, the invitation (*pravāraṇā*) is also on the fifteenth day. I, the monk of such-and-such a name, declare myself to be pure regarding the obstructing factors (*antarāyika-dharma*). I announce my purity regarding the invitation; and having announced it, I make it known. Thus a second time, and thus a third time.
Regarding the monk who bestows the invitation (*pravāraṇā*): if he bestows the invitation through a bodily intimation (*kāyavijñapti*), it should be declared that the invitation has been bestowed.
If he bestows it through a vocal intimation (*vāgvijñapti*), it should be declared that the invitation has been bestowed. If he bestows it through both a bodily intimation and a vocal intimation...

The invitation (*pravāraṇā*) must be declared. One does not grant it through a physical gesture (*kāyavijñapti*) nor through a verbal intimation (*vāgvijñapti*). Either the entire Saṃgha must go there, or that monk must be brought into the midst of the Saṃgha. If the entire Saṃgha does not go there and they do not bring that monk into the Saṃgha, yet they proceed with discord, they commit an offense of transgression (*sātisāra*).
If the monk who is giving the invitation (*pravāraṇā*) does not proceed by undertaking the rules of customary conduct as they have been prescribed, he becomes guilty of an offense.
Monks, I shall prescribe the rules of customary conduct for the monk who receives the invitation. By the one who receives the invitation...
Having accepted the invitation (*pravāraṇā*), a monk must not run, nor gallop, nor leap;

he must not leap over a moat, nor leap over a terrace; he must not stand in the air above, nor go outside the boundary, nor ascend two steps of a ladder with one foot, nor two rungs of a staircase with one foot.

One should mount [the vehicle], but one must not sleep nor enter meditative absorption. One who sleeps or enters absorption becomes blameworthy for two reasons: because of a lack of shame and because of negligence. (Pravā-v J 4.5.1)

When the senior of the Saṃgha says, "Venerable ones, announce your consent (*chanda*) and your purity (*pāriśuddhi*) so that you do not have to come; and report that they have been announced," he should stand before a neighboring monk and say: "Pay attention, Venerable One: in such-and-such a residence, there is a monk who is afflicted, suffering, and gravely ill. Today is the Saṃgha’s invitation (*pravāraṇā*)."
The fifteenth-day [observance].

For that monk as well, the *pravāraṇā* is on the fifteenth day. This monk, named so-and-so, performs the *pravāraṇā* by means of three grounds: what is seen, what is heard, and what is suspected. His consent for the *pravāraṇā*—

And I announce the *pravāraṇā*, and I make known that it has been announced. If a monk who is the receiver of the *pravāraṇā* does not proceed by undertaking the rules of proper conduct (*āsamudācārika-dharma*), he becomes guilty of an offense. (GBM 6.1054.1–2; MSV,Wi 43).
*Pravā-v* J 4.6.

The Venerable Upāli asked the Buddha, the Blessed One: "Venerable Sir, if a monk who has been appointed as the receiver of the *pravāraṇā* should, after receiving the *pravāraṇā*, die right there, should it be said that the *pravāraṇā* was brought back or not brought back? "It was not brought back, Upāli; it must be brought back again. [If] the monk who has been appointed as the receiver of the *pravāraṇā*, Venerable Sir, [should die] after receiving the *pravāraṇā*...

Having taken it, he arrives in the midst of the Saṃgha and should pass away. It should be declared that the *pravāraṇā* has been brought, even if it has not actually been brought. "It has not been brought, O Upāli," [he says].
"It must be brought again.
(Pravā-v J 4.7)

He claims to be a householder; he claims to be a novice monk (*śramaṇoddeśaka*); he is a *ṣaṇḍhaka*; he is a *paṇḍaka*; he is one who has violated a nun; he is a matricide; he is a patricide; he is a murderer of an Arhat; he is a schismatic of the Saṃgha; he is one who has shed the blood of a Tathāgata with malicious intent; he is a heretic; he is one who has entered into the fold of heretics; he is a thief living in communion [with the Saṃgha].
He acknowledges being of a different residence or not being in communion. It should be stated whether the invitation (*pravāraṇā*) has been brought or not brought.
"It has not been brought, Upāli; it must be brought again."
In the *Pravāraṇāvastu*, J 5.1.1,
the Venerable Upāli asks the Buddha, the Blessed One:
"Venerable Sir, regarding a monastery where a single monk resides..."

Therefore, how should that very [monk] conduct himself on the fifteenth day of the Pravāraṇā ceremony? Upāli, that monk should sprinkle the monastery, sweep it, and apply a fine coating of cow dung. He should prepare a lion-throne and arrange seats. He should provide the hearing of the Dharma.
Then, afterwards, one should look in the four directions from a higher place.
(Pravā-v 153)
J 5.1.3.1. If monks who are pure and of like views arrive, they should be addressed as follows: "Venerable ones, please come very quickly; today is the *pravāraṇā* of the Saṃgha."

The fifteenth-day [Pravāraṇā]. The Pravāraṇā of me, a monk of such-and-such a name, is also on the fifteenth day. I, the monk of such-and-such a name, today perform the Pravāraṇā before the Venerable Ones by means of three grounds: what has been seen, what has been heard, and what is suspected.
Thus a second time, and thus a third time.
Pravā-v J 5.1.3.2.
If it is accomplished, that is well. If it is not accomplished, that monk, having sat down on his own seat, should generate this thought and speak these words: "Today..."
The Saṃgha’s invitation ceremony (*pravāraṇā*) is on the fifteenth day. For me as well, the monk named so-and-so, the invitation ceremony is on the fifteenth day.

Therefore, I, the monk named so-and-so, now for this day, resolve upon the invitation ceremony. I shall invite [the Saṃgha] by means of what has been seen, heard, or suspected. Thus a second time, and thus a third time.
Pravā-v 5.2.

Where two monks reside, there this same sequence must be followed in informing one another. Where three monks reside, there too the sequence must be followed in informing one another. Where four monks reside...
Having made a formal motion (*jñapti*), they should perform the invitation ceremony (*pravāraṇā*). However, a monk should not be appointed as the presiding inviter (*pravāraka*).
(Pravā-v 5.3.1) Where five monks reside, [they should perform the ceremony].

Having made a formal motion (*jñapti*), they should perform the invitation ceremony (*pravāraṇā*). A monk should be appointed as the inviter (*pravāraka*). However, the invitation of one who is ill must not be accepted.
Pravā-v 5.3.2.

Wherever six or more monks reside, they should perform the invitation ceremony (*pravāraṇā*) after having made a formal motion (*jñapti*). A monk should be appointed as the presiding officer for the invitation (*pravāraka*). The invitation of one who is ill should be accepted on his behalf.
Uddāna 3. Intermediate summary verse.
An unrighteous *pravāraṇā* should be set aside with a single utterance.
For in what [case] is there indeed a single utterance? It is when the formal act (*kriyā*) has been undertaken.
Pravā-v 6.1.
One suspension of the *pravāraṇā* is lawful (*dhārmika*), one is unlawful (*adhārmika*), and three suspensions of the *pravāraṇā* are lawful.
One is unrighteous. Five are righteous suspensions of the *pravāraṇā*, and one is unrighteous. (GBM 6.1053.1; MSV,Wi 44).
Pravā-v 6.2.1.
What is the one righteous suspension of the *pravāraṇā* and the one unrighteous? (GBM 6.1053.2; MSV,Wi 44).
Pravā-v 6.2.2.

When the *pravāraṇā* by a single proclamation is being uttered and has not yet been concluded, if one suspends the *pravāraṇā*, it is a lawful suspension of the *pravāraṇā*. (GBM 6.1053.2; MSV,Wi 44).
Pravā-v 6.2.3.
When speech has been uttered and concluded, one suspends the *pravāraṇā*; this is an unrighteous suspension of the *pravāraṇā*.
Thus, among these, there is one righteous suspension of the *pravāraṇā* and one unrighteous [suspension]. (Pravā-v 6.2.4; GBM 6.1053.3; MSV,Wi 44)
(Pravā-v 155) (Pravā-v 6.3.1.
There are three lawful suspensions of the *pravāraṇā* and one unlawful one. Which is it? (GBM 6.1053.3; MSV,Wi 44)

In the case of a *pravāraṇā* consisting of two recitations, if one suspends the *pravāraṇā* while the first recitation is being spoken and not yet concluded, that suspension of the *pravāraṇā* is in accordance with the Dharma.
Pravā-v 6.3.2.2.
When the first speech has been spoken and concluded, one suspends the *pravāraṇā*; this is a suspension of the *pravāraṇā* that is in accordance with the Dharma.
Pravā-v 6.3.2.3.

When the second speech has been uttered but not yet concluded, he suspends the *pravāraṇā*; this is a lawful suspension of the *pravāraṇā*. (Pravā-v 6.3.3) When the second speech has been uttered and concluded, he suspends the *pravāraṇā*; this is an unlawful suspension of the *pravāraṇā*.
Pravā-v 6.3.4:
Thus, these three are suspensions of the invitation ceremony (*pravāraṇā*) that are in accordance with the Dharma, and one is not in accordance with the Dharma.
Pravā-v 6.4.1:
There are five lawful ways of suspending the *pravāraṇā* ceremony and one unlawful way. What is the [lawful] suspension?

During a *pravāraṇā* consisting of three proclamations, when the first proclamation is being recited and has not yet concluded, if one suspends the *pravāraṇā*, this is a lawful suspension of the *pravāraṇā*.
When the first speech has been spoken and concluded, one suspends the *pravāraṇā*; this is the lawful suspension of the *pravāraṇā*.
(Pravā-v 156) When the second speech has been spoken but not yet concluded, he suspends the invitation (*pravāraṇā*); this is a righteous suspension of the invitation. (GBM 6.1053.6; MSV,Wi 44)
Pravā-v 6.4.2.4.

When the second speech has been spoken and concluded, he suspends the invitation (*pravāraṇā*); this is a suspension of the invitation that is in accordance with the Dharma. (GBM 6.1053.6; MSV,Wi 44).
Pravā-v 6.4.2.5.
When the third recitation has been spoken but not yet concluded, he suspends the *pravāraṇā*; this is a lawful suspension of the *pravāraṇā*.
Pravā-v 6.4.3.
When the third recitation has been spoken and concluded, he suspends the *pravāraṇā*; this is an unlawful suspension of the *pravāraṇā*. (GBM 6.1053.7; MSV,Wi 44)
Pravā-v 6.4.4:
These five are the suspension of the *pravāraṇā* that are in accordance with the Dharma, and one is not in accordance with the Dharma. (GBM 6.1053.7; MSV,Wi 44).
Pravā-v 7.1.
There is a Pravāraṇā with one recitation, a Pravāraṇā with two recitations,
and a Pravāraṇā with three recitations.
The invitation for the community. For what purpose is the invitation by a single proclamation?
Summary 4. Intermediate summary.
Arśā and Varṣā are kings; Madhura is the determination of the Dharma.
The Saṃgha has fallen into an obstacle; this is the group that has been gathered together.
It may happen that on the very fifteenth day of the invitation ceremony (*pravāraṇā*), many monks...
(Pravā-v 157) Pravā-v 7.2.1.1.2.
In that regard, it occurs to the monk who is the *pravāraka* as follows: "Today is the fifteenth-day invitation (*pravāraṇā*) of the Saṃgha."
And these many monks...
[If] I were to perform the invitation ceremony (*pravāraṇā*) by means of a threefold proclamation, [it would be difficult for them to understand].
"Suppose I were to perform the *pravāraṇā* by means of a single proclamation. He performed the *pravāraṇā* by means of a single proclamation;
in this sense, it is called the "single-proclamation *pravāraṇā*."

For *Pravā-v* 7.2.1.2.1–7.2.1.8.1, the Sanskrit text of the manuscript (folio 70) is lost. The extant text is from a fragment of the *Pravāraṇāvastu* of the Mūlasarvāstivādins from the Turfan Collection (SHT VI 1578).

In another case, there is a *pravāraṇā* with a single proclamation. This occurs when, on that very fifteenth day of the *pravāraṇā*, many bedding and seats have been placed out in the open air, and the rain begins to fall... (SHT VI 1578r1).

In that regard, it occurs to the monk who is the *pravāraka* (the one conducting the invitation): "Today is the fifteenth-day *pravāraṇā* of the Saṃgha. Furthermore, many bedding and seats have been placed out in the open air, and the sky is raining... (SHT VI 1578r2-3).
If I were to perform the invitation ceremony by means of the threefold proclamation,
I would not be able to have the bedding and seats prepared without becoming damp.

"What if I were to perform the invitation ceremony (*pravāraṇā*) by means of a single proclamation? He then performed the invitation ceremony by means of a single proclamation. In this matter, it is the "single-proclamation" invitation ceremony.

In another case, there is a *pravāraṇā* with a single proclamation. For example, on that very fifteenth day of the *pravāraṇā*, the king comes to the monastery together with his queens, princes, ministers, military officers, and the people of the towns and countryside. The king has bestowed upon the Saṅgha an abundant gift of robes and material requisites; likewise by the queens...

Furthermore, the princes, ministers, military commanders, and the people of the towns and countryside gave him abundant gifts of clothing and material goods. And by the monk who was the proclaimer, he was proclaimed... (SHT VI 1578r4-v1).

In that regard, it occurs to the monk who is the *pravāraka*: "Today is the fifteenth-day *pravāraṇā* of the Saṃgha. And the king, together with his queens, princes, ministers, military officers, and the people of the towns and countryside, comes to the monastery. The king has bestowed upon the Saṃgha a great abundance of robes and material gifts; so too have the queens and the princes."

The ministers, the elite of the army, the merchants, and the country folk gave him an abundant gift of robes and material offerings. And by the monk who was the proclaimer, he was proclaimed... (SHT VI 1578v2-3).

"If I were to perform the invitation (*pravāraṇā*) by means of a threefold proclamation, I would not be able to complete the invitation. What if I were to perform the invitation by means of a single proclamation? He then performed the invitation by means of a single proclamation. In this sense, there is the "single-proclamation" invitation.

There is a *pravāraṇā* (invitation to criticism) consisting of a single proclamation regarding another matter. For example, on that very fifteenth day of the *pravāraṇā*, thieves may plunder a village, a city, or a town. Having arrived at the gate of the monastery (*ārāma*), they kill a cow or a buffalo.
Or, having made goats with blood-stained limbs and blood-smeared bodies, they send a messenger to the monks, saying:
"May the noble ones depart; we shall dwell here.
In that regard, it occurs to the monk who is to perform the *pravāraṇā*: "Today is the fifteenth-day *pravāraṇā* of the Saṃgha. Yet bandits are plundering a village, or a city, or a market town.
Having come to the gate of the monastery, they have killed a cow, a buffalo, or a goat, and are now [making] blood-stained limbs and blood-smeared marks."
Having done so, they send a messenger to the monks, saying: "May the venerable ones depart; we shall dwell here.
If I were to perform the invitation ceremony with the threefold proclamation..."
"Because of this, there might be an obstacle to my life, an obstacle to my state of a recluse, or an obstacle to my holy life.
What if I were to perform the invitation ceremony with a single proclamation? He then performed the invitation ceremony with a single proclamation.
In this context, it is called the "single-proclamation invitation."

Regarding another matter, there is a formal invitation (*pravāraṇā*) consisting of a single proclamation. For instance, on that very fifteenth day of the invitation ceremony, some elderly, foolish, deluded, unintelligent, or unskilled person [might cause] a woman of a household [to appear] in the vicinity or on the path leading to the vicinity.

Or a noble maiden may be reviled, addressed with harsh words, or even assaulted. Enraged men, having come to the gate of the monastery, will shout out as they seize those captured: "Seize these Śramaṇas, the daughters of the Śākyas!
Kill them! Bind them! Exile them! They shall become the king’s elephant-riders, horse-riders, brick-climbers, and flag-bearers!"
Or those who mount the banners. They will perform various royal duties and royal affairs. (GBM 6.724.2-4; MSV IV 119.7-14). Pravā-v 7.2.1.9.2.
In that regard, it occurs to the monk who is the *pravāraka* (the one who invites criticism): "Today is the fifteenth-day invitation (*pravāraṇā*) for the Saṃgha. By someone else..."

And by that old man, who was foolish, dull-witted, and unskilled, a woman of good family or a maiden of good family was either reviled, addressed, or touched in the vicinity or on the path to the vicinity. Enraged men came to the gate of the monastery and proclaimed against those who had been seized:
"Seize these śramaṇas, sons of the Śākyas! Kill them! Bind them!"

Let them be sent away. They shall become elephant-riders for the king, or horse-riders, or brick-climbers, or flag-climbers, or banner-climbers. They shall perform various royal duties and royal tasks.

"If I were to perform the invitation ceremony with three proclamations, it might lead to an obstacle to my life, an obstacle to my state as a śramaṇa, or an obstacle to my holy life. Suppose, then, that I were to perform the invitation ceremony with a single proclamation. He then performed the invitation ceremony with a single proclamation.
In this matter, the invitation (*pravāraṇā*) is performed with a single proclamation (*ekavācikā*). (GBM 6.724.6–7; MSV IV 120.2–6).
In another matter, the invitation is performed with a single proclamation. For instance, when a monastery has been established in a region inhabited by non-human beings (*amanuṣya*).
And by a certain elderly, foolish, deluded, unlearned, and unskilled person, excrement, urine, spittle, snot, vomit, or purgings were discarded in an unsuitable place,
or a bed or seat was cast down and defiled with impurities. Consequently,
non-human beings became enraged and remained in his dwelling area, on the path to his dwelling area, on his walking path, and even in his latrine.
They enter even the gateway chambers; they enter the monks' quarters as well,
and they overturn the couches.

In that regard, it occurs to the monk who is to perform the *pravāraṇā*: "Today is the fifteenth-day *pravāraṇā* of the Saṃgha. Furthermore, this monastery has been established in a region inhabited by non-human beings. And by a certain elder who is foolish, deluded, ignorant, unskilled, and improper, [it has been placed] in an unsuitable location. (Pravā-v 161)

Excrement, urine, spittle, snot, vomit, or purgings have been cast away, or the bedding and seats have been smeared with impurities. Enraged non-human beings (amanuṣya) dwell even within the monastery precincts, on the paths through the precincts, on the walking-paths, in the pens, and even in the gate-chambers. They also enter into the monks.
They even turn over their beds. (GBM 6.724.8-9; MSV IV 120.12-14).
"If I were to perform the invitation ceremony with the threefold formula..."
"Because of this, there might be an obstacle to my life, an obstacle to my state of a recluse, or an obstacle to my holy life.

Suppose, then, that I were to perform the invitation ceremony with a single proclamation. He performed the invitation ceremony with a single proclamation. In this sense, it is called the "invitation ceremony with a single proclamation."

There is a formal invitation (*pravāraṇā*) consisting of a single proclamation regarding another matter. For example, when a monastery has been established in a location inhabited by wild beasts, and some senior monk who is immature, foolish, ignorant, unskilled, or incompetent [places it] in an unsuitable location.

Excrement, urine, spittle, snot, vomit, or purgings have been cast away, or the bedding and seats are smeared with impurities. Furious beasts of prey remain in the precincts, on the path to the precincts, on the walking-path, in the enclosure, and even in the gateway chamber; they even enter upon the monks.
They even turn over the beds.
